Short of time? Read the key takeaways.

🧠 Trauma is usually remembered, not repressed. Traumatic events are far less likely to be forgotten than ordinary ones. And if you have forgotten one, techniques like hypnosis are more likely to produce a false reconstruction than a true memory.

📝 Recovering forgotten memories often means reconstructing them. The brain fills gaps with plausible predictions that feel real. Many students who described learning of the Challenger disaster later recalled it very differently, yet felt extremely confident in their new versions.

🧩 Finding the root cause isn't the same as healing. Knowing immediate causes of your problems (such as depression being partly caused by seeing yourself as fundamentally unlovable) can be valuable. Tracing that belief back to childhood can feel like solving a satisfying puzzle, but understanding alone doesn't create change.

🛠️ Effective therapies often skip the origin story. Cognitive behavioral therapy, backed by hundreds of randomized controlled trials, tends to focus on present symptoms. Exposure therapy reduces phobias without exploring their cause. Most treatments don't focus on origin stories (with PTSD treatment being a notable exception).

😤 Venting rarely reduces anger. Shouting or punching a punching bag may seem like it should feel cathartic, but it doesn't change how you see the person or situation. What actually reduces anger includes breathing, understanding the other person's perspective, and forgiving them.

There are so many popular misconceptions about human psychology. We got a lot of positive feedback for our previous article and video on this topic, so today we're digging back in. We’re here to dispel 3 more very popular myths about human psychology.
And just like last time, you can choose your own adventure: either read the newsletter version below, or watch the video version of this newsletter by clicking here.
When something really traumatic occurs, do people repress those memories? And do techniques like recovered memory therapy and hypnosis bring those memories back again?

Why might people believe this is true? Well, it's certainly true that we forget almost everything that happens to us. Our memories are not like camcorders; we're not simply recording all the events in sequence. Instead, we're compressing the information.

Imagine trying to figure out what you ate 17 Thursdays ago for dinner. Chances are you have no memory whatsoever of that event. So then, you might argue traumatic events are just like anything else. We forget the vast majority of what happens to us. So, we might forget traumatic events as well. And then you might think we need special techniques in order to get these memories back.

There are actually two problems with this line of thinking. The first is that traumatic events (unlike ordinary events) such as what you ate for dinner one day, are actually far less likely to be forgotten. You're much more likely to remember a situation where something terrible happened to you than a situation where you just sat down and had an ordinary dinner.
The second issue is the claim that you can use special techniques to recover that lost memory. This is where things get really worrisome.

It's true that we sometimes temporarily forget things. For instance, you might forget the name of that celebrity and then get it back again by reminding yourself of movies they were in. If you've actually forgotten something, attempting to pull back that memory is actually likely to cause you to reconstruct it. That means your brain will actually predict missing details and fill them in as though you're actually remembering them. Sometimes this reconstruction is perfect (e.g,., you may have perfectly remembered the celebrity's name), but other times it's not. And unfortunately, we can't tell the difference between memories that we're actually recalling exactly as they were and reconstructed predictions that didn't actually occur.

In fact, memory in general involves prediction and reconstruction. Imagine you're trying to recall the home that you lived in when you were 5 years old. You might remember some actual things about that home, but other details you might not remember, like what the curtains looked like; but if you're trying to visualize the home in your mind (and you're not aphantasic), the curtains will be there. It's just that your brain might be predicting what they look like based on the color themes and other aspects of the home rather than literally remembering them.

The problem is we can't reliably tell the difference. It can be very difficult to tell whether we actually remember what the curtains look like or if our brain is reconstructing the curtains based on what's plausible, given the actual memories there. Both of these are likely to feel the same.

In fact, this idea can be shown experimentally. On our website ClearerThinking.org, we have a free tool called “Is Your Memory Like a Photograph?” and in it, with your permission, we can create a harmless memory of something someone never actually witnessed. You can try it out for free here:
The Space Shuttle Challenger Memory Experiment

A fascinating and famous example of how memory reconstruction works was demonstrated after the space shuttle Challenger exploded. Psychologists Ulric Neisser and Nicole Harsch conducted an experiment where (the day after the Challenger disaster) they asked their students to write down what they were doing and where they were when they found out about the space shuttle disaster.

After roughly 3 years had elapsed, they then had those same students write down what they remembered about what they were doing when the space shuttle exploded. The shocking thing is that many of these memories that they wrote down were really different from what they'd written down on the day of the actual disaster. On top of that, the participants were extremely confident in their newer, incorrect ‘memories’ – some even insisted that the new versions were correct.
Image shows the front page of the book chapter that describes the Challenger memory experiment, with some relevant text highlighted.
The claim that memories can be accurately reconstructed by going through a systematic procedure can be a dangerous one.
We saw some horrendous examples of this happen during the “satanic panic,” in the 1980s and 90s.

Some people believed that something horrible had happened to them, but didn't know what it was. Using hypnosis or memory reconstruction techniques, they tried to get themselves to remember these bad events. Some of them ended up reconstructing memories that they’d been abused in a satanic ritual.

Not only were some of these stories totally implausible, but when police investigated them, they found a total lack of evidence. It now seems very likely that many of these memories were false. As you can imagine, this was very damaging to those who had come to believe false, disturbing things about their past. This included causing severe damage to their relationships with other people in their lives and even caused some people to be falsely imprisoned.
Image shows an article about George Franklin Sr. who was wrongfully imprisoned as a result of false beliefs about memory reconstruction.

It's important to be nuanced about the relationship between trauma and memory. While it is true that we're much more likely to remember traumatic things than we are to remember ordinary things, we can forget traumatic events just like we can forget anything else – particularly if we didn’t recognize the events as traumatic at the time.

It is also true that people sometimes consciously suppress traumatic memories. That is, these memories are so upsetting that when they come to mind, people try to immediately put them out of their minds, and sometimes even try to deny that they ever happened.

Interestingly enough, when people have PTSD, they often struggle not to think about the traumatic event that caused it. The event actually pops into their minds much more often than they’d like (including in the form of nightmares, flashbacks, and distressing reactions to reminders of the event), rather than being suppressed.

Unfortunately, events that are potentially traumatic are really quite common. Even if we just take a single category like sexual abuse, depending on the estimation method, we find that something like 10% to 30% of girls under the age of 18 in the US have been sexually abused (estimates vary with different definitions and methods). Almost all of these events of claimed sexual abuse are genuine; they're not fictitious memories or lies.

If a traumatic event happens to you, very likely you will remember it. But if you don't remember it, using a method to try to reconstruct the details is, unfortunately, more likely to lead to a false reconstruction than a true one.
Myth 2: Knowing the Root Cause Cures Mental Health Issues

Does knowing why you have a mental health challenge help you get better in the long term? That is, if you can identify which specific events caused your mental health challenge (whether it's traumatic events or the way your parents treated you or other childhood experiences), does that mean you'll actually get better from those mental health challenges? Well, first let's explore why people might believe this.

It's certainly true that a deep understanding of the causes of a problem can help you solve it. If your clock isn't working, it's very important to understand whether it's the gears that are broken or it's simply out of battery.

However, it's not necessarily helpful to know why the gears are broken. It doesn't matter whether it was because it was dropped, because your cat jumped on it, or because they were installed badly. As long as you know that the gears are broken and how, that's all you need to know to fix it.

For mental health, it's similar. It can be very valuable knowing the immediate causes of your mental health challenges. For instance, realizing that your depression stems from viewing yourself as fundamentally unlovable and unworthy. It is typically much less useful to know the distant causes. For instance, whether viewing yourself as unlovable came about because of the way your parents treated you or came about because of your bullying as a child doesn't necessarily matter, as long as you understand that it's the perception of unlovability that's contributing so much to your depression.

Another reason people might think it's important to figure out the events that led you to have the mental health challenges that you do is that it can be extremely satisfying to do so. It feels like you're solving a puzzle (“Wow! So, that's the reason I am the way I am today.”). However, solving that puzzle doesn't automatically make you feel better. You simply understand why you are that way, but you haven't yet done the work to actually change.
But how do we actually know that you don't have to understand the originating events in order to treat a mental health problem? Well, we can see it in the data.

Cognitive behavioral therapy is one of the most studied therapies in the world, with literally hundreds of randomized controlled trials demonstrating its effectiveness for treating different mental disorders. And remarkably, it doesn't focus on the originating events that cause people to be the way they are. It focuses on the way people are today and treating their symptoms. And it does so quite successfully. Let's illustrate this with an example.

Suppose that when you were young, you were on a flight that was extremely scary due to bad weather, and you developed a phobia of flying from this experience. Now, there's a really good chance you'd remember this event (if you're young enough, you may have actually forgotten it) but still may have that fear of flying today. So, what's the most effective treatment for phobias like this? Well, it's not uncovering the originating event. In fact, some people with phobias will know exactly what that originating event is, and yet they'll still have the full phobia.

One of the most effective ways to reduce anxiety in the long term is to use exposure therapy – which doesn't explore the original cause at all! This is a therapy where the person is exposed again and again to the thing they fear in a safe environment and typically without the use of “safety” behaviors like avoidance, distraction, or seeking reassurance. (For a more detailed discussion of exposure therapy and some tips on how to do it, see this article of ours.)

Let's be nuanced about this. Is it ever useful to understand the originating event in order to improve your mental health? Well, it absolutely can be useful when it gives you insight into the immediate causal effects. For example, if understanding that:
the reason you hate yourself is that your parents always put you down (that’s the originating event)
the things you say to yourself in moments of acute self-hatred are versions of the ways they put you down (and they’re the immediate causal effects)
then that better understanding of the origins of your self-hatred might be useful for treating your depression.

But overall, the most effective methods for treating mental health disorders usually don't require understanding the originating events. The notable exception is therapy focused on treating PTSD, where the most effective approaches do focus on the initiating event (note: contrary to Myth 1, those therapies aim to change how you process the traumatic event, rather than trying to uncover repressed parts of it).

It’s a really good thing that effective treatment typically doesn’t require understanding originating events because, if we have forgotten those originating events, there's really no good way that we're going to be able to reconstruct them!

Does shouting at someone or punching a punching bag because you're so angry make you less angry? For example, you’ve probably heard about the idea of “getting your anger out.” Some people even say it's healthy to pay money to go to a rage room so you can break things to really express your anger.
Image shows people in a “rage room”

Why might people believe this is true? When we're really angry and we express it, such as by shouting at someone or punching a punching bag, it tends to feel good, and it feels like we're making progress; like some kind of catharsis is happening.

My favorite metaphor for emotions is to think of them like the beeping of a smoke detector. We have an emotion system analogous to a smoke detector, but it's trying to detect when certain situations occur instead of smoke. The emotion itself is like the beeping of the smoke detector. It's telling you that something is happening that may matter, giving you important information. If you learn to ignore the smoke detector in your house, that could pose a real risk when there's a fire. If you learn to ignore all your emotions, you're also missing out on critical information.

So, what does anger represent the detection of? Prototypically, anger is what we experience when we think that someone is purposely trying to harm or disrespect us, or harm something else that we value. But we can also experience anger at things we don’t think are intentional, when they get in the way of our goals or seem unfair (e.g., anger at a computer crashing or at a billing error that charges you more than other people for a service).

Anger often gets a bad rap, and that's because it can cause a lot of problems. Our anger can lead another person to get angry, which can lead us to be even more angry. It can lead to verbal fights and saying things you don't really mean. It can even lead to physical fights and physical danger. On social media, anger can be a total disaster. It can lead us to get fixated on the words of people we hate. And it can lead us to say things that we regret.

But anger can also have a lot of value. It's often telling us important information. In prototypical cases, it tells us that we believe that someone is trying to harm or disrespect us or jeopardize something that we value. For instance, we might feel anger at the idea of injustice, and it can motivate us to try to improve the world or to stop bad actors. And anger when someone's trying to take advantage of us can help us assert our boundaries and stay protected. It demonstrates to others that they won't get away with harming us.

With all this in mind, let's go back to the question of what actually reduces anger rather than maintaining it. If you believe someone's trying to take advantage of you or do injustice in the world or harm someone you love, simply shouting at them or punching a punching bag is not going to change your perspective on them or the situation. So, long term, it's not going to shift your anger.

One thing that actually shifts anger is understanding. If you come to understand that the person is not actually trying to harm you, and you see where they're coming from, that will actually be likely to make you less angry. Another thing that can reduce anger is forgiveness. Even if you understand that the person was trying to cause that harm, if you forgive them for it, you'll tend to become less angry.

What about expressing your anger? Well, that can actually go either way. If someone does something that you think is harmful to you and you express that to them angrily, there are different possibilities. One possibility is that they say they're sorry or explain their reasoning, and through that you actually become less angry. Another possibility is that they escalate or justify their selfish actions or become angry back, and you actually become more angry as a result. So, whether expressing anger increases it or reduces it depends on how the other person acts and how you react to how they react.
Sometimes people learn not to notice their own anger, or not express it. Becoming more aware of it and learning to express it can certainly be helpful.

But when we vent our anger by punching a punching bag or shouting at someone, we're not actually doing anything to change the anger long term. The most effective routes I know of to reduce anger in the long term include truly understanding something from another person's perspective and completely forgiving them. In the short-term handling of anger, CBT-based anger management and slow breathing have evidence in their favor.
Why We Believe These Psychological Myths
What do these psychological myths we covered today have in common? These are all examples of psychological ideas that are appealing, despite not actually being helpful.
It's appealing to think that if we just use the right method, we can reconstruct those missing memories.
It's appealing to think that if we just figure out the originating events of our mental health challenges, the mental health challenges will go away.
It's appealing to think that if you express your anger or shout at someone, that's cathartic and going to fix your anger.
But rarely are any of these true.
